stare: Old Town: Market Square and Barbican

Warsaw's historic centre, razed by the Germans in 1944 and rebuilt after the war from period paintings and prints, which is why it's on the UNESCO list. The market square has colourful houses and the statue of the Mermaid, the city's symbol; a little further north is the Barbican, the 16th-century brick bastion.
zamek: The residence of the Polish kings at the end of Castle Square, destroyed in 1944 and rebuilt in the 1970s with money from the Polish people. Inside are the royal apartments, the Throne Room, the Knights' Hall and Matejko's great historical paintings; Sigismund's Column on the square is Warsaw's meeting point.
krakowskie: The main avenue of the Royal Route, running south from the Castle past churches, palaces and the University: here are the Presidential Palace, the Holy Cross Church, which keeps Chopin's heart in a pillar, and the historic Bristol café. Further south it continues as Nowy Świat, the street of cafés and shops.
sasski: Piłsudski Square and the Saxon Garden

The great square where the Saxon Palace stood until 1944: only a few arches remain, sheltering the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier with its guard of honour. Behind the square is the Saxon Garden, an 18th-century public park with avenues and fountains, a short walk from Krakowskie Przedmieście.
pkin: The 237-metre Stalinist skyscraper, a gift from the Soviet Union to Poland completed in 1955, which dominates the centre. From the 30th-floor terrace you see the whole city; Varsovians say it has the best view because it's the only place you can't see the building itself.
powstanie: The museum devoted to the Warsaw Uprising of August–October 1944 against the German occupation, in a former power station. With sounds, photos and objects, it recreates 63 days of fighting in which about 200,000 civilians died: a long and at times harrowing visit, with an entrance that takes your breath away.
polin: POLIN Museum of the History of Polish Jews

The museum of the history of Jews in Poland, a thousand years of shared life from the Middle Ages to the Holocaust and today, built on the site of the former Warsaw Ghetto. In front stands the 1948 Monument to the Ghetto Heroes. The glass building and the permanent exhibition deserve time and attention.
lazienki: Łazienki Park and the Palace on the Isle

Warsaw's most beautiful park, 76 hectares, the summer residence of Poland's last king, Stanisław August. The neoclassical Palace on the Isle stands in the lake, surrounded by gardens, theatres, an amphitheatre, peacocks and squirrels; the Chopin monument is by the Aleje Ujazdowskie entrance.
wilanow: King John III Sobieski's Baroque residence, south of the city, the "Polish Versailles": a yellow palace that survived the war almost intact, with apartments, portraits and a large Italian- and English-style garden.
praga: The district on the right bank of the Vistula, which was not destroyed in 1944 and keeps its period courtyards and façades. Koneser is the old vodka factory turned into a centre with restaurants and shops, and Ząbkowska Street is full of bars and murals.
